definition: In antitrust law, the rule of reason is a general system of analysis used to determine whether restraints of trade that are not per se unlawful, violate Section 1 of the Sherman Antitrust Act. To establish a claim under Section 1 of the Antitrust Act, the plaintiff generally must show: 1. A concerted agreement between two or more parties; Rule in Shelley's Case / rule of reason Dictionary compilation | 26 September 2026 2. That resulted in an unreasonable restraint of trade; and 3. The unreasonable restraint of trade affected interstate commerce. Under Section 1, certain contracts, combinations, or conspiracies that unreasonably restrain foreign or interstate commerce are per se unlawful. Examples of per se unlawful agreements include:  Certain horizontal price-fixing schemes  Some collusive group boycotts  Bid rigging  Market allocation agreements In most cases, the alleged anticompetitive behavior does not fit into one of the per se categories and is subsequently subject to judicial interpretation under the rule of reason standard. The rule of reason doctrine asks whether the restraint “merely regulates and perhaps thereby promotes competition or whether it is such as may suppress or even destroy competition.” See Board of Trade of City of Chicago v. U.S., 246 U.S. 231 (1918). To answer the question, a fact dependent inquiry into the context of the restraint is often required. Today, the commonly accepted method is a burden shifting framework that places the initial burden on the plaintiff to show the defendant's behavior has or will harm competition in the “relevant market.” The application of the rule of reason often requires a case-by-case contextual definition of the relevant market. See Ohio v. American Express Co., 585 U.S. 529 (2018). Plaintiffs can show harm to competition through direct or indirect evidence. Direct evidence includes reduced output, increased prices, and decreased quality in the relevant market. Indirect evidence requires proof of market power in the relevant market along with evidence that the defendant’s behavior could harm competition. See Tops Markets, Inc. v. Quality Markets, Inc., 142 F.3d 90 (2d Cir. 1998).
